newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Gold - Australia shrugs at crackdown.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Gold - Australia shrugs at crackdown.

text.p: South Korea's crackdown on speculative gold traders is curtailing the flow of gold in Asia, although Australian gold producers are seeing little in the way of higher physical prices.

Premiums on Australian bullion landed in Hong Kong continue around US$0.30 cents an ounce over the London spot price, little changed since July, when the South Korea government took strong measures to discourage the country's booming gold transhipment business.
"That's still relatively cheap," a gold dealer said.
A view among buyers of physical gold that the metal was unlikely to trade out of its current range of around $385.00 an ounce has made any efforts to lift premiums a hard sell.
"Gold's going nowhere. That's been made pretty clear in recent days when even U.S. attacks on Iraq failed to have a moving effect," said one commodities analyst.
Australia's local jewellery fabrication industry also has been relatively untouched by the events in South Korea, since nearly all the gold it uses is purchased domestically.
South Korea's gold imports in July fell 49.6 percent to $335 million from $665 million in June, while exports over the same period declined 50.9 percent to $318 million, trade ministry figures show.
The level of actual physical gold circulating in Asia will probably decline now that less gold is stopping off in South Korea.
Profits from arbitrage opportunities were so high, the South Koreans were willing to pay otherwise prohibitive shipping costs to get their hands on bullion.
"The way they were getting cheap funding, they didn't care where they were getting the gold from," said Mark Freemantle, senior bullion dealer for Rothschild Australia Ltd.
"It just had to touch the dock to be re-exported," he said.
Bullion houses were importing huge amounts of gold on 90-day deferred payment, immediately re-exporting the metal and parking the proceeds in high interest domestic money market instruments.
Bullion dealers reaped huge profits from arbitrage between local interest rates of more than 11 percent and London Interbank Offered Rate of around five percent.
On July 1, the government shortened the deferred payment period to a maximum 30 days.
That, plus a depreciation of the Korean won against the dollar, made gold trading unprofitable for all but the biggest houses dealing in huge quantities.
